patient_information: A 32-year-old man from Malawi with a past medical history notable for an episode of a blistering and painful skin lesion on the right side of his abdomen three years prior, which healed spontaneously and was suspected to be herpes zoster.
chief_complaint: Pain in the right upper abdomen and a feeling of faintness, especially when standing.
history_of_present_illness: The patient was well until one month prior to admission when he began to experience a feeling of fullness in his upper abdomen. In the week before admission, he developed pain in the right upper abdomen, which was particularly apparent when sleeping on his right side. He recently started to feel breathless on lying down and faint upon standing and walking.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from Malawi. The clinical context notes that in Africa, tuberculosis is the most common cause of pericardial effusion and there is a strong association between tuberculosis and HIV infection.
vitals: Pulse was regular at 130 bpm with a pronounced pulsus paradoxus measured at 15 mmHg. Blood pressure in the supine position was 90/60 mmHg. He was slightly breathless in the supine position.
physical_exam: The patient was thin. His jugular venous pulse appeared elevated, the apex beat was impalpable, and heart sounds were quiet without murmurs. Chest auscultation was normal. Examination of the abdomen revealed an enlarged, tender, palpable liver measured at 8 cm below the right costal junction. There was also evidence of mild peripheral oedema of the legs and sacral area.
labs_and_diagnostics: Haemoglobin was 10.5 g/dL and the white blood cell count was 9.8 G/L. A chest radiograph showed an enlarged globular heart with clear lung fields. A therapeutic pericardial aspiration yielded 500 mL of bloodstained pericardial fluid. An HIV test was subsequently found to be positive.
differential_diagnosis: The primary clinical syndrome was identified as pericardial tamponade from a large pericardial effusion. The differential diagnosis for the cause in this African setting included tuberculosis, other bacterial infections, malignancy, and HIV-related Kaposi’s sarcoma. Given the history of a likely herpes zoster attack, HIV-associated tuberculosis was considered the most probable diagnosis.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent therapeutic pericardial aspiration, with 500 mL of fluid removed, leading to an immediate increase in blood pressure to 120/80 mmHg. He was started on standard first-line antituberculous treatment (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months) and prednisolone at 60 mg daily, tapered over ten weeks. Following a positive HIV test, antiretroviral therapy was started four weeks after commencing antituberculous treatment. He made a full and uneventful recovery.
final_diagnosis: The patient was diagnosed with HIV-associated tuberculous pericarditis complicated by a large pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade. The diagnosis was based on the classic clinical signs of tamponade (tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, hypotension), radiographic evidence of a globular heart, a history suggestive of immunosuppression (herpes zoster), a positive HIV test, and a complete response to pericardial drainage and empiric antituberculous therapy.
